title: Gilgamesh and Enkidu: The Wrestle
subtitle: They meet as enemies and end as the first friendship in literature

learningObjectives.text: How do Gilgamesh and Enkidu meet?

meeting.work: An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic
meeting.author: Anonymous
meeting.translator: Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay
meeting.locator: Pennsylvania Tablet · Column VI · part 2; Pennsylvania Tablet · Column VI · part 2, normalized characters 105-738
meeting.excerpt: They met in the plaza of the district. Enkidu blocked the gate With his foot, Not permitting Gish to enter. They seized (each other), like oxen, They fought. The threshold they demolished; The wall they impaired. Gish and Enkidu Seized (each other). Like oxen they fought. The threshold they demolished; The wall they impaired. Gish bent His foot to the ground, [149] His wrath was appeased, His breast was quieted. When his breast was quieted, Enkidu to him Spoke, to Gish: "As a unique one, thy mother bore thee. The wild cow of the stall, [150] Ninsun, Has exalted thy head above men. Kingship over men Enlil has decreed for thee.
meeting.note: Verbatim translation from the named Old Babylonian tablet witness in this edited edition. Brackets and question marks signal textual restoration or uncertainty.

narrativeBlocks.title: At the bride's door
narrativeBlocks.body: Enkidu blocks Gilgamesh from claiming another bride — and the king of Uruk, unbeaten, meets his match. They wrestle in the street until the city's walls shake.

narrativeBlocks.title: Mutual recognition
narrativeBlocks.body: Gilgamesh wins — barely — and something unexpected happens: the two strongest beings in the world look at each other and stop. They embrace and become inseparable friends.

narrativeBlocks.title: The purpose of an equal
narrativeBlocks.body: The gods' design works exactly as planned: Gilgamesh's excess energy finally has somewhere to go — partnership instead of tyranny. The city gets relief; the king gets a brother.

narrativeBlocks.title: Restlessness follows
narrativeBlocks.body: But two strong men idle is its own problem. Gilgamesh proposes a fame-quest: the Cedar Forest and its guardian Huwawa. Enkidu warns him it is dangerous — and goes anyway, because that is what friends do.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why the friendship matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Gilgamesh is the first epic where the emotional core is a bond between two men, not a conquest or a romance. Enkidu's coming death — the grief that drives the second half — lands only because this friendship is real.
